```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

import pathlib
import json
import duckdb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

ROOT = pathlib.Path(".").resolve()  # analysis/
DATA = ROOT.parent / "data"
DB_PATH = ROOT.parent / "evictions.db"

# --- Load neighborhood features (December 2024 ETL output) ---
df = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "outputs" / "neighborhood_features.csv")
df["neighborhood"] = df["neighborhood"].str.strip()

# --- Load owner eviction data ---
owners = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "outputs" / "owner_eviction_counts.csv")
owners["owner"] = owners["owner"].str.strip()

plaintiff_map = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "outputs" / "plaintiff_to_owner.csv")
plaintiff_map["sdat_owner"] = plaintiff_map["sdat_owner"].str.strip()
plaintiff_map["plaintiff"] = plaintiff_map["plaintiff"].str.strip()

# --- Load neighborhoods GeoJSON ---
gdf = gpd.read_file(DATA / "neighborhoods.geojson")

# Merge GeoDataFrame with feature table
gdf = gdf.merge(df, left_on="Name", right_on="neighborhood", how="left")

# Export merged GeoJSON for plotly (need feature id = Name)
geo_dict = json.loads(gdf[["Name", "geometry"]].to_json())
for feature, row in zip(geo_dict["features"], gdf.itertuples()):
    feature["id"] = row.Name

# --- Load full-year monthly data from DB ---
con = duckdb.connect(str(DB_PATH), read_only=True)
monthly = con.execute(
    "SELECT strftime(CAST(event_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS month, "
    "COUNT(*) AS warrants FROM warrant_filings GROUP BY month ORDER BY month"
).df()
con.close()

# --- Key summary stats ---
dec_warrants = int(df["eviction_count"].sum())
year = monthly["month"].str[:4].iloc[0]
year_total = int(monthly["warrants"].sum())

# --- Shared style ---
PLOTLY_TEMPLATE = "plotly_white"
MAPBOX_STYLE = "carto-positron"
MAP_CENTER = {"lat": 39.2904, "lon": -76.6122}
MAP_ZOOM = 10
COLOR_SEQ = px.colors.sequential.Reds
```

## The Scale of the Problem

In **`{python} year`**, Baltimore City courts issued **`{python} f"{year_total:,}"` eviction warrants** — roughly **`{python} f"{year_total // 12:,}"` per month** on average. The chart below shows how that volume shifted across the year.

```{python}
#| label: monthly-trend

fig = px.bar(
    monthly,
    x="month",
    y="warrants",
    labels={"month": "Month", "warrants": "Eviction Warrants Filed"},
    template=PLOTLY_TEMPLATE,
    color_discrete_sequence=["#c0392b"],
)
fig.update_layout(
    title="Eviction Warrants Filed by Month — Baltimore City 2024",
    xaxis_title=None,
    yaxis_title="Warrants Filed",
    margin=dict(t=50, b=40),
    height=380,
)
fig.show()
```

*The detailed neighborhood and landlord analysis in the sections below is based on December 2024 data (`{python} dec_warrants` warrants), where address geocoding and court record matching are most complete.*

---

## A Different Framework

Most conversations about eviction focus on tenant behavior — missed payments, lease violations. But the *where* of eviction tells a different story.

Eviction rates in Baltimore track almost perfectly with a set of conditions that tenants didn't choose: what neighborhood they were born in, whether it was redlined in the 1930s, how concentrated landlord ownership is in their block. These are **social determinants of eviction** — upstream structural forces that predict who gets a warrant served at their door.

This analysis maps those forces at the neighborhood level — Baltimore's 279 neighborhoods — using December 2024 court data spatially joined to neighborhood boundaries and merged with Census P3/P4/P12/H1/H4 demographic data and SDAT property records.

---

## Where Evictions Happen

```{python}
#| label: eviction-map

fig = px.choropleth_mapbox(
    gdf,
    geojson=geo_dict,
    locations="Name",
    color="eviction_rate_per_1k_hh",
    color_continuous_scale=COLOR_SEQ,
    mapbox_style=MAPBOX_STYLE,
    center=MAP_CENTER,
    zoom=MAP_ZOOM,
    opacity=0.75,
    hover_name="Name",
    hover_data={
        "eviction_count": True,
        "eviction_rate_per_1k_hh": ":.1f",
        "Name": False,
    },
    labels={
        "eviction_rate_per_1k_hh": "Warrants per 1k HH",
        "eviction_count": "Warrants (Dec 2024)",
    },
)
fig.update_layout(
    title="Eviction Warrant Rate by Neighborhood (December 2024)",
    margin=dict(t=50, b=0, l=0, r=0),
    height=520,
    coloraxis_colorbar=dict(title="Warrants<br>per 1k HH"),
)
fig.show()
```

The clustering is not random. High-rate neighborhoods form a pattern that should be familiar to anyone who has studied Baltimore's geography of inequality.

---

## Overlapping Geographies

Eviction maps and racial composition maps in Baltimore look nearly identical — not because race causes eviction, but because both reflect the same underlying history of segregated investment and disinvestment.

```{python}
#| label: side-by-side-maps

fig1 = px.choropleth_mapbox(
    gdf,
    geojson=geo_dict,
    locations="Name",
    color="eviction_rate_per_1k_hh",
    color_continuous_scale=COLOR_SEQ,
    mapbox_style=MAPBOX_STYLE,
    center=MAP_CENTER,
    zoom=9,
    opacity=0.75,
    hover_name="Name",
    labels={"eviction_rate_per_1k_hh": "Warrants per 1k HH"},
)
fig1.update_layout(
    title="Eviction Rate",
    margin=dict(t=40, b=0, l=0, r=0),
    height=420,
    coloraxis_colorbar=dict(title="Warrants<br>per 1k HH"),
)
fig1.show()

fig2 = px.choropleth_mapbox(
    gdf,
    geojson=geo_dict,
    locations="Name",
    color="pct_black",
    color_continuous_scale="Blues",
    mapbox_style=MAPBOX_STYLE,
    center=MAP_CENTER,
    zoom=9,
    opacity=0.75,
    hover_name="Name",
    labels={"pct_black": "% Black"},
)
fig2.update_layout(
    title="% Black Residents",
    margin=dict(t=40, b=0, l=0, r=0),
    height=420,
    coloraxis_colorbar=dict(title="% Black"),
)
fig2.show()
```

> **Note:** A third map showing 1930s HOLC redlining boundaries would complete this comparison. Those boundaries are available from the [Mapping Inequality project](https://dsl.richmond.edu/panorama/redlining/) — overlay them and the three maps are nearly coextensive.

## What the Data Shows

Each dot below represents one of Baltimore's 279 neighborhoods (filtered to those with at least 100 residents). The relationships are not subtle.

### Race and Eviction

```{python}
#| label: scatter-race

fig = px.scatter(

    x="pct_black",
    y="eviction_rate_per_1k_hh",
    hover_name="neighborhood",
    trendline="ols",
    template=PLOTLY_TEMPLATE,
    labels={
        "pct_black": "% Black Residents",
        "eviction_rate_per_1k_hh": "Warrants per 1,000 HH",

)

fig.show()
```

## Who Is Doing the Evicting

A small number of landlords account for a disproportionate share of eviction filings. The 20 entities below filed the most warrants in December 2024.

```{python}
#| label: top-evictors-bar

top20 = owners.head(20).copy()
top20["owner_label"] = top20["owner"].str.title().str.strip()

fig = px.bar(
    top20.sort_values("eviction_count"),
    x="eviction_count",
    y="owner_label",
    orientation="h",
    template=PLOTLY_TEMPLATE,
    labels={
        "eviction_count": "Warrants Filed (Dec 2024)",
        "owner_label": "",
    },
    title="Top 20 Landlords by Eviction Warrant Count — December 2024",
    color="eviction_count",
    color_continuous_scale=["#fadbd8", "#c0392b"],
)
fig.update_layout(
    height=560,
    margin=dict(t=60, l=250, b=40),
    showlegend=False,
    coloraxis_showscale=False,
)
fig.update_traces(
    text=top20.sort_values("eviction_count")["eviction_count"],
    textposition="outside",
)
fig.show()
```

### Court Name → SDAT Owner Matching

Court filings often use abbreviated or alternate names. The table below shows the top plaintiffs as they appear in court records alongside the matched SDAT property owner.

```{python}
#| label: plaintiff-table

top20_map = plaintiff_map.head(20).copy()
top20_map.columns = ["Court Filing Name", "Warrants", "SDAT Owner", "Units Matched"]
top20_map = top20_map.reset_index(drop=True)
top20_map.index += 1

top20_map.style \
    .set_table_styles([
        {"selector": "thead th", "props": [("background-color", "#2c3e50"), ("color", "white"), ("font-weight", "bold")]},
        {"selector": "tbody tr:nth-child(even)", "props": [("background-color", "#f9f9f9")]},
        {"selector": "td, th", "props": [("padding", "6px 12px"), ("text-align", "left")]},
    ]) \
    .bar(subset=["Warrants"], color="#c0392b", vmin=0)
```

---

## What This Means

The data points to three levers for reducing eviction in Baltimore:

1. **Ownership concentration** is among the strongest predictors of eviction rates in the data. Policies that disperse ownership (community land trusts, right-of-first-refusal for tenants, LLC transparency requirements) address the root structural driver.

2. **A small number of landlords** account for a disproportionate share of filings across all 279 neighborhoods. Targeted intervention — whether mediation programs, inspection priority, or rental registry enforcement — can reach a large fraction of evictions by focusing on 20 entities.

3. **The data infrastructure to do this work is improving but incomplete.** December 2024 is the month where geocoding and court record matching are most complete. A fully geocoded, real-time eviction dataset — publicly accessible — would let advocates, journalists, and policymakers track these patterns continuously rather than after the fact.

Eviction is not an inevitable consequence of market conditions. It is a policy choice, made building by building, court date by court date. The geography of that choice is visible in the maps above.
